summary:
Puerto Rico is a United States territory, and the United States federal framework applies on the island in full: federal statutes, executive orders and agency procedure govern entry, documents, screening, federally funded care and federal custody. Puerto Rico's own legislation does not soften that framework, and in the area of trans medical care it sharpens it.

United States travel documents record sex assigned at birth, and Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, eliminated the X marker, so a trans visitor arriving on United States documents may present a marker that does not match their appearance at inspection. Entry scrutiny is tightened further for one category of traveller: in February 2025 the United States State Department announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

Airport screening at Puerto Rico's airports follows federal Transportation Security Administration procedure. All luggage is screened and may be hand-searched. Prosthetics, including breast forms, are treated as medically necessary equipment rather than liquids, so they fall outside the three-liquid rule and are allowed through the checkpoint after screening. Published guidance for trans travellers advises packing strategies that reduce the likelihood of invasive searches.

In July 2025 Puerto Rico banned gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, barred public funding for that care, and set penalties of up to 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine and permanent loss of medical licences for doctors who violate the ban. The Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court.

The care law was pushed through non-public hearings and is written with deliberate vagueness, so doctors and affirming parents who facilitate hormone treatment or top surgery risk prosecution. It mandates campaigns by the Education and Health departments on the risks of trans-affirming care. Health Secretary Ramos Otero proposed amendments that would have allowed puberty blockers and the continuation of existing hormone treatment, but the text as enacted stands as the most restrictive care law in any United States jurisdiction according to the report documenting it.

Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics, and the territory is also covered by the United States federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. The first hate crime charges in Puerto Rico's history were brought in 2020, after Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged in the murder of two transgender women on 22 April 2020; Bonilla confessed to the killings. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island.

Anti-discrimination coverage remains partial. The 2013 law that passed (Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013) was amended in the House to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities, housing, transit and business transactions are not covered by it. An earlier bill, House Bill 1725, passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 with wider coverage but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved.

Marriage recognition for same-sex couples in Puerto Rico was obtained through the federal courts: four couples joined the federal lawsuit filed in March 2014, with Lambda Legal and Puerto Rico Para Todas intervening, and plaintiffs included a couple married in Canada in 2007 and another married in New York in 2012, one of them a former National Guard member.

Under Executive Order 14168, which directs United States federal agencies to recognise only two sexes, the Bureau of Prisons houses transgender inmates by sex assigned at birth rather than asserted gender identity, a rule that governs any federal custody in Puerto Rico. The ACLU said it had received reports that transgender women were being transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or moved to solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting how many transgender people it holds. Advocates say the order contravenes the Prison Rape Elimination Act requirement that trans inmates' housing be decided by individual safety assessment.
tangentialFactors:
Conversion-therapy and religious-freedom legislation has been a recurring flashpoint. In March 2019 the pro-statehood caucus in the Puerto Rico House blocked a floor vote on Senate Bill 1000, which would have banned conversion therapy for minors, despite Senate passage and the governor's support, with co-sponsor Senator Zoe Laboy dissenting publicly. In April 2019 Governor Ricardo Rosselló announced a pair of bills, Senate Bills 1253 and 1254, one framed as clarifying religious freedom principles and the other as a conversion-therapy ban carrying a pastoral exemption for clergy; LGBT council president Johanne Velez Garcia and allied advocates said the pairing would open doors to discrimination on orientation and gender-identity grounds, and the governor asked lawmakers to withdraw the bills on 13 June 2019 amid sustained opposition.

A 2017 religious-freedom bill that would have permitted public businesses to refuse service to LGBTQ people was vetoed by Governor Rosselló in February 2018, and a similar 2019 bill was withdrawn after House approval amid protests.

The care law's standing as the most restrictive in any United States jurisdiction places Puerto Rico at one extreme of a wider national pattern of restrictions on trans medical care, while its hate-crime and emergency-declaration record places it among the territories that have formally recognised violence against trans residents as a state-level problem.

Puerto Rico's Penal Code retained a sodomy prohibition upheld by the Puerto Rico Supreme Court in 2002 until the United States Supreme Court's Lawrence v. Texas ruling in 2003, after which the territory amended the code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute. The provision concerned consensual conduct rather than conduct that would expose a trans visitor to enforcement.
localsOnly:
House Bill 488, signed 29 May 2013, extended domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity, giving residents a protection route independent of the employment-only anti-discrimination law.

The mandates on the Education and Health departments to run campaigns on the risks of trans-affirming care affect residents directly: school and health-system messaging in the territory will carry the state's position on trans care, and the enacted law's vagueness exposes affirming parents as well as clinicians to prosecution.

Residents under 21 lose access to publicly funded gender-affirming care under the July 2025 statute, and clinicians face permanent licence loss in addition to criminal penalties, which constrains the local pool of providers regardless of a patient's ability to pay privately.

Residents in federal custody are housed by sex assigned at birth under the Bureau of Prisons rule, with reports of transfers to men's prisons and of placement in solitary confinement, and the agency no longer publishes counts of transgender people in its custody.
outOfScopeNotes:
No separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections policy on trans-inmate housing, special-unit provision, or judicial ruling on the issue was located in the sources, so territory-level custody practice beyond the federal rule remains unresolved.

The sources do not state whether the Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation filed its announced court challenge to the July 2025 care ban, or how any such litigation has proceeded; the case status is unresolved.

The sources do not report the outcome of the 2020 hate-crime prosecutions of Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla, nor what measures followed the January 2021 state of emergency declaration.

Whether the 2013 employment-only anti-discrimination statute has been used successfully by trans complainants, and whether federal employment protections supply the gaps in housing, transit and public facilities, is not sourced here.
